prompt: What goes at the top of the inverted pyramid?
hint: The one sentence you would keep.

choices.text: The topic of the presentation
choices.why: "Today I'll talk about first deliveries" tells the room what is coming without telling it anything.

choices.text: The finding, together with what you want done
choices.why: A reader who stops there has the news and the request.

choices.text: A teaser that builds suspense
choices.why: It spends the room's best minute on waiting.

choices.text: The method, so the room trusts what follows
choices.why: Method sits at the narrow end, read by few.

prompt: Why did newspapers adopt the inverted pyramid, by the lesson?
hint: Editors and readers both cut from the bottom.

choices.text: Stories cut from the bottom survived, and readers stopped early
choices.why: Both reasons point the same way: put the weight at the top.

choices.text: It was the only shape the presses could print
choices.why: The reasons given are editing and reading, not printing.

choices.text: Readers preferred suspense
choices.why: The shape exists because they did not wait.

choices.text: Journalists were paid by the paragraph
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so.

prompt: Marina's finding arrives at minute nine of eleven. What risk does the lesson name?
hint: Attention falls, and meetings run over.

choices.text: That the slides run out of space
choices.why: Space is not the issue; timing is.

choices.text: That the room finds it too surprising to accept
choices.why: Surprise is the case for holding the answer back, a different situation.

choices.text: Some of the people who matter never hear it
choices.why: Somebody leaves, or the meeting cuts the last minutes.

choices.text: Sandra presents her own analysis first, before Marina has had a chance to speak
choices.why: Not in the story; the risk is about attention and time.

prompt: Order the inverted pyramid from top to bottom.
Why does presenting in the order of the work feel right to an analyst?

choices.text: It is the order the audience asked for
choices.why: Nobody asked; the analyst is answering an unspoken question.

choices.text: It shows care and postpones being challenged
choices.why: Both motives backfire: trust comes from the evidence and the answers, after the finding.

choices.text: Slide tools number slides in that order
choices.why: Software numbers slides in whatever order you give.

choices.text: Because methodology is legally required to come first in any company report
choices.why: No such rule exists.

prompt: In Marina's first deck, on which slide did the link between late first boxes and cancellations first appear?
Where does the lesson say the journey of the analysis can go instead? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The appendix
choices.why: Slides nobody sees unless they ask.

choices.text: A methods note sent with the deck
choices.why: For the people who will check the work.

choices.text: The answer to "how did you get there?"
choices.why: One sentence, with the appendix slide ready.

choices.text: The first ten minutes
choices.why: That is the trap itself.

prompt: Which piece of the journey does belong near the start?
hint: Something the room will think of anyway.

choices.text: How the tables were joined
choices.why: Nobody in the room is waiting for that.

choices.text: The months that were excluded from the data and the reasons for each one
choices.why: A caveat for the appendix or the methods note.

choices.text: The tools you used
choices.why: Interesting to analysts; not a question the room has.

choices.text: A dead end the room will think of
choices.why: Saying early that region does not explain it saves the question, and it is evidence rather than chronology.

prompt: Lesson 2 puts the recommendation last; this lesson puts the conclusion first. How do they fit?
hint: One is the order of the argument.

choices.text: They do not; pick one per audience
choices.why: Both apply to every audience.

choices.text: Announce it in one sentence, argue in order, ask at the end
choices.why: The first sentence is a promise; the four parts keep it.

choices.text: The recommendation moves to the start and the context to the end
choices.why: The argument keeps its order; only the one-sentence answer is added up front.

choices.text: The conclusion is shown first only in emails, never in meetings
choices.why: The lesson applies answer-first to presentations too.

prompt: Put the five moves of an answer-first presentation in order.
BLUF stands for bottom line up ___.
When does the lesson allow holding the answer back?
hint: Uncomfortable is not the same as unbelievable.

choices.text: Whenever the finding is uncomfortable for someone in the room
choices.why: Most findings are uncomfortable and can still lead.

choices.text: When the audience is senior
choices.why: Seniority is a reason to lead with it.

choices.text: When the conclusion will be rejected on sight
choices.why: Then state the question first and let the evidence bring the room to the answer.

choices.text: When there is time for questions at the end of the meeting
choices.why: Time for questions does not change what the room should know first.

prompt: What happens to a request that arrives as a surprise, by the lesson?

choices.text: It is approved faster
choices.why: The opposite: people want time.

choices.text: It is rejected outright
choices.why: The lesson's risk is delay, not rejection.

choices.text: Nothing, because surprise helps the room remember
choices.why: Memory is not the problem; deciding is.

choices.text: It gets postponed to next month
choices.why: People need time to think about it, and that time is how decisions slip.

prompt: A presentation has two governing thoughts. What does Minto's first rule say?

choices.text: Put the more important one first
choices.why: Order does not fix two tops.

choices.text: They are two talks
choices.why: Two talks, or you have not yet found the idea that joins them. One tree, one top.

choices.text: Merge them with "and"
choices.why: Two ideas joined by "and" are still two.

choices.text: Present them on alternate slides
choices.why: That splits attention.

prompt: MECE: mutually exclusive and collectively ___.
"Late deliveries cause churn" and "customers dislike waiting" sit side by side as reasons. What is wrong?

choices.text: Nothing; both are true
choices.why: True is not enough: they repeat each other.

choices.text: They are the same reason twice
choices.why: They overlap, so the group is not mutually exclusive.

choices.text: The second needs a number
choices.why: A number would not remove the overlap.

choices.text: They are in the wrong order, since the effect should come before the cause in the group
choices.why: Swapping them leaves the same overlap.

prompt: A branch of your pyramid has no evidence under it. What have you found?

choices.text: A gap in the analysis, before the room finds it
choices.why: That is the pyramid's main use before the slides.

choices.text: A reason to add more slides
choices.why: Slides without evidence are decoration.

choices.text: A sign that the governing thought is wrong
choices.why: Not necessarily; the reason may be true and still unproven.

choices.text: A detail for the appendix, to be shown only if somebody in the room asks about it
choices.why: The appendix holds evidence; this branch has none.

prompt: Which subject line can Paulo act on from his inbox?

choices.text: First-delivery analysis
choices.why: It says an analysis exists.

choices.text: Interesting finding on churn
choices.why: It says you find it interesting.

choices.text: Decision by Friday: 8-week pilot to cut late first deliveries
choices.why: Longer, and the only one that carries the request and the deadline.

choices.text: Re: re: churn
choices.why: A thread nobody can place.

prompt: Which questions make up the headline test? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Does a reader who sees only this know what I found?
choices.why: The finding.

choices.text: Do they know what I want from them?
choices.why: The request.

choices.text: Is it under ten words?
choices.why: Length is not the test; the useful subject line was the longest.

choices.text: Does it contain a number?
choices.why: Useful often, and not the test.

prompt: A reader stops after two sentences of Marina's email. What should they still be able to do?

choices.text: Explain the method
choices.why: Method is at the narrow end.

choices.text: Quote every number
choices.why: Two sentences carry the key numbers only.

choices.text: Find the attachment in the email thread
choices.why: Not the test.

choices.text: Reply "approved"
choices.why: The finding, the request and what approval involves are all in the first two sentences.
